About this document


This document provides the teaching content for History Years 11–13 of the New
Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being published
separately.

Progress and assessment information for History Years 11–13 is still in development.
Once that is completed, History Years 11–13 is proposed to be made by the Minister
of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the
Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer History Years 11–13 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from 1
January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year 13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

Students are taught core historical concepts, knowledge, and practices that explain
how people, societies, cultures, and environments have changed and interacted over
time. Through the use of historical sources, evidence, narratives, and disciplinary
concepts, students examine causes and consequences, continuity and change,
significance, perspectives, and contestability. They investigate how historical events,
decisions, movements, and experiences have shaped communities, nations, and
societies, and how interpretations of the past vary across contexts and over time.
History provides students with the knowledge and practices to investigate historical
questions, sources, events, issues, and interpretations using disciplinary concepts,
methods, and evidence. This disciplinary knowledge helps students develop the
ability to apply historical thinking to interpret information, analyse relationships and
patterns, evaluate evidence and perspectives, explain historical developments, and
construct informed understandings of the past in local, national, regional, and global
contexts.
As students progress through Years 11–13, they develop the ability to evaluate and
synthesise historical information, perspectives, interpretations, and evidence, and to
communicate well-reasoned conclusions using disciplinary language and conventions
in written form. This enables them to construct and justify historical arguments,
assess the reliability and significance of evidence, consider differing interpretations,
and communicate thoughtfully and effectively about complex historical issues and
their contemporary relevance.

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.

 In History, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to construct and communicate historical explanations, interpretations, and arguments by selecting, analysing, and evaluating evidence for
 specific purposes and audiences.

The Historical Significance strand requires the selection of a teacher-selected topic.
The topic descriptor appendices provide guidance and considerations to support
teachers when making this selection, ensuring the chosen context enables students
to develop the intended historical knowledge and practices.

Māori and Indigenous histories

When teaching Māori histories, teachers must engage with the relevant Māori
knowledge and practice statements within the teaching sequence. These statements
are specific to Māori contexts and cannot be substituted. Programmes should
recognise the significance of mātauranga Māori, Māori perspectives, and Māori
historical experiences, and support engagement with these histories in culturally
responsive and respectful ways. For Indigenous groups, sources that include
depictions or descriptions of people who are now deceased may require a caution.

Where Māori knowledge is used, appropriate permissions, relationships, attribution,
and tikanga must be respected.

Responsible use of artificial intelligence

Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative
processes, but it may also introduce bias, inaccuracies, ethical concerns, and issues
relating to ownership. AI should enhance, not replace, critical or creative thinking,
source evaluation, subject knowledge, or students’ own analysis and decision-
making. Responsible AI use emphasises the importance of exercising independent
judgement, drawing on credible sources, verifying information, being transparent
about AI use, considering diverse perspectives, and developing independent thinking.

Year 12: Historically significant event or movement
Teachers should avoid selecting a topic that substantially duplicates learning from
other topics within the year’s programme. The selected topic should provide distinct
opportunities for students to apply and develop the knowledge and practices
contained within the Historical Significance strand. The selected context should be
significant to New Zealand or a Realm of New Zealand nation and provide
opportunities to examine changing interpretations, meanings, and judgements of
significance.

Historical significance
The focus should be on why an event or movement is significant, the changes it
produced, and how its significance may vary between perspectives.

Examples of events and movements that may be suitable to explore include:

•   The women’s suffrage movement, associated with democratic participation,

•   The Battle of Ōrākau, associated with the New Zealand Wars, resistance,

Historical Significance
Year 13: Shifting significance
Teachers should avoid selecting a topic that substantially duplicates learning from
other topics within the year’s programme. The selected topic should provide distinct
opportunities for students to apply and develop the knowledge and practices
contained within the Historical Significance strand. The selected context should be
significant to New Zealand or a Realm of New Zealand nation and provide
opportunities to examine changing interpretations, meanings, and judgements of
significance.

Historical significance
Suitable contexts enable students to investigate how significance can change across
time, places, cultures, and communities. Students should have opportunities to
analyse how events, movements, people, and places have been interpreted,
remembered, commemorated, or overlooked, and how memory, commemoration,
identity, beliefs, relationships, evidence, and perspectives shape competing
judgements about their significance.

Examples of topics that may be suitable to explore include:

•   Parihaka, associated with Māori resistance, land confiscation, and changing
    understandings of nonviolent resistance.
•   The Dawn Raids, associated with migration, discrimination, Pacific peoples, and
    changing understandings of historical significance.
•   The Mau movement, associated with Samoan self-determination, colonialism,
    nonviolent resistance, and changing interpretations of New Zealand’s role in
    Samoa.
